title: the crossing of the Yamuna
hook: a baby cries in the prison, Kamsa comes running, and the child he reaches for slips out of his hands into the sky
carry: stop killing the helpless for nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday Vasudeva left his son beside sleeping Yashoda and carried her daughter back into the prison. Your line was he returns with empty arms.

A newborn cries in the cell. The guards jerk awake and run to the king. Kamsa leaps out of bed, the Bhagavata says, hair loose, stumbling, and rushes to the prison. This is the eighth child, the one the voice warned him about at the wedding. Devaki holds the baby close and begs him. It's a girl, a daughter of your own house. Don't kill a girl. You've taken so many of my children. Leave me just this one. Kamsa doesn't hear her. He tears the child out of her arms.
screen: `A CRY IN THE CELL.` → `KAMSA RUNS TO THE PRISON.` → `"IT'S A GIRL. LEAVE ME THIS ONE."`

segments.voice: He swings the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone, and she slips out of his grip. She rises into the air, and she is no longer a baby. The Bhagavata calls her the younger sister of Vishnu: a goddess with eight arms, holding weapons, in garlands and bright clothes, with celestial beings singing her praise. And she speaks down to him. What will you gain by killing me, fool? The one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Stop killing the helpless for nothing. Then she is gone. The text says she came to be worshiped on earth in many places, under many names. Kamsa grabbed the one child who could not be harmed, and the attempt only revealed the truth. The crossing worked. The boy is safe across the river, and now even Kamsa knows it. Then, for a moment, Kamsa breaks. He frees Devaki and Vasudeva from their chains. He apologizes, even weeps, and says that everyone acts under fate, and that he has been cruel. Devaki and Vasudeva forgive him. A gentle moment, from Kamsa of all people. It doesn't last. The next morning his ministers advise that, if the child is out there somewhere, newborns across the land should be hunted. Kamsa agrees. The goddess told him to stop killing the helpless. He heard it, and chose fear anyway.
screen: `SHE SLIPS FROM HIS GRIP` · `THE GODDESS WITH EIGHT ARMS` · `"YOUR KILLER IS BORN ELSEWHERE"` · then, large: `KAMSA FREES THEM, THEN CHOOSES FEAR`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one fear that keeps steering you, even after you've seen it clearly. Breathe in and name it to yourself, simply; breathe out and let your grip on it loosen, even a little, the way the child slipped from Kamsa's hands. If you pray, you can offer that fear in your prayer.
Yogamaya. The Lord's own power, born as Yashoda's daughter, who rises from Kamsa's hands as a goddess and tells him the truth.
Your line: stop killing the helpless for nothing. Tomorrow, a stranger comes to Gokula. That's day eight hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Bhagavata honor the girl born to Yashoda as Yogamaya, a form of the Goddess, and in some places she is worshiped as a sister of Krishna.

chat.says: What happened to the baby girl Kamsa grabbed in the prison?
options: She slipped from his grip and rose as a goddess, warning him his killer lived.
Vasudeva snatched her back and hid her safely with Yashoda in Gokula.
Kamsa took pity on her and sent her home to be raised in his palace.
chat.meaning: She was Yogamaya. She slipped from Kamsa's hands, rose with eight arms, and told him his killer was already born.

Yogamaya.meaning: the Lord's own power, born as Yashoda's daughter

Vishnu.meaning: the great god; the goddess is called his younger sister

Kamsa.meaning: the king who fears Devaki's eighth child

Devaki.meaning: Krishna's birth mother, in Kamsa's prison

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.4: the guards wake, Devaki's plea, the girl slips from Kamsa's hands and appears as the eight-armed goddess, her words, Kamsa's remorse, the ministers' counsel

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm: Devaki's plea (a girl, his niece, the last one), the eight arms and weapons (10.4.10), her words (10.4.12), and the text's statement that she became known by many names in many places.
The ministers' advice is summarized; the text specifies which infants; confirm.
Kamsa's appeal to fate and the parents' forgiveness are summarized; confirm.
howItsDone: some regional traditions identify Yogamaya with Vindhyavasini or with Subhadra/Ekanamsha as Krishna's sister; kept general. A Keeper should check the wording.
Editor pass: hook no longer calls the scene 'the morning after'; the text sets it the same night, with the ministers' counsel the next morning.

Audit (2026-10-01): Devaki's plea (10.4.4) calls the girl snusha, a daughter-in-law of his house, and asks him not to kill a woman; 'she's your niece' was a gloss not in the text, so the plea now follows the verse more closely. Match prompt 'the morning after' contradicted the same-night setting; changed. Cut the stock line 'what makes this scene so sharp'.
